number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 1, Number finally upheld: 1
key_evidence_accepted: The testimony of PWs-1 and 3 was convincing and natural, and their statement was accepted as reliable. The statement of the deceased under Section 161 CrPC was treated as a dying declaration under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act. The recovery memo disclosed the recovery of rubber gloves used by the appellant, and the chemical report confirmed the presence of acid on the gloves.
witness_credibility: PWs-1 and 3 were total strangers and their presence was justified in every respect. They were not interested in the deceased and their version was accepted as truthful and natural. Their credibility was not challenged as they were not shown to be stock witnesses.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 26.05.1980; Trial judgment: 06.09.1982; High Court decision: 28.11.2008; Supreme Court decision: 06.12.2012
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: M.P. Shorawala, Jyoti Saxena, Ranbir Yadav, Anzu K. Varkey and Shashi Kiran; Counsel for the State: Ratnakar Dash, Alka Sinha and Anuvrat Sharma
investigation_status: FIR registered u/s.326 /PC; Statement of victim u/s.161 CrPC; Death of the victim one day thereafter; Case altered to that u/s.302 /PC; Charge sheet filed; Trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Section 302, IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment; High Court: Affirmed the conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution case was that PWs 1 and 3 saw the accused-appellant sprinkling acid on the body of 'Y' who suffered extensive burn injuries. FIR was registered against the appellant under Section 326 IPC. PW-4 recorded the statement of 'Y' under Section 161 CrPC. 'Y' died one day after the incident. Thereafter the case was altered to that under Section 302 IPC. The trial Court convicted the appellant under Section 302, IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment.
defence_argument: The substantial contention made on behalf of the appellant was that PW1 and 3 could not have witnessed the incident and that having regard to the nature of the injuries sustained by the deceased 'Y', he could not have made a statement under Section 161 Cr.P.C. It was further contended on behalf of the appellant that even if the statement can be said to have been made by the deceased, the same cannot be treated as a dying declaration for non-fulfillment of the statutory requirements and that absence of the acid marks on the accused belied the case of the prosecution. One other submission made on behalf of the appellant was that PWs -1 and 3 were stock witnesses and, therefore, their version could not have been relied upon.
legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle that a statement made by a person who is dead or cannot be found is relevant under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act, and that such a statement can be treated as a dying declaration even if it was recorded under Section 161 CrPC, provided it meets the criteria of a dying declaration.
precedent_relied_upon: Jai Prakash and Others v. State of Haryana 1998 (7) SCC 284; Ravikumar alias Kutti Ravi v. State of T.N. 2006 (9) SCC 240
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution case was established by abundant legal evidence, and the Court found the statement of the deceased as a dying declaration to be true and voluntary, thus justifying the conviction under Section 302 IPC.
